question: Do the commands say of the same bytes what the policy of the exit codes has them say, whatever the bytes? Where they did not, is it put right, and does putting it right change the verdict of any stream that exists?
method: `oadec_fuzz::parity` puts one stream to every command that reads one, through the calls of `oadec_cli::api`: `info`, `verify`, `verify --decode`, `oamd`, `emdf`, `decode` to samples of presentations 0 to 3 (or of the programme and the core of an AC-3 family stream), and `decode` to a DAMF set and to an ADM file. `check` holds the answers to `docs/exit-codes.md`, clause by clause. Beside the campaign, `examples/flips.rs` changes every bit of each of its streams in turn, puts the checksums right and asks the same. The campaign (`crates/oadec-fuzz/tests/campaign.rs`) takes 86 short streams, runs of the ten fixtures and of the 76 streams `oadec-synth` writes, changes one with the seeded mutations of the crate, puts its checksums right in three rounds of four, and asks. Before anything was changed, a tally of 60 000 rounds over the fixture runs alone showed what the commands said as they were. The object outputs put every Object Audio Metadata payload on a timeline, which refuses one without an object element and one of another programme than the first; `verify` now makes the same refusals through `oadec_spatial::PayloadCheck`, which is the check the timeline makes. `oamd --json` counted the payloads of every stream of the work directory that would be refused. `tools/old_new.py --decode-all` compared the binary of main before the change with the change.

counted_and_not_claimed.a_change_no_command_noticed: with the checksums put right, a change to the samples is caught by the lossless check of its restart interval, which the restart header after it carries. The streams of the campaign are a few access units long and most changes fall after their last restart header, which nothing but the parity and the CRC of a segment covers. So most rounds that every command called clean decode to other samples than their seed. An AC-3 family stream has no check but its CRCs at all. This is what putting the checksums right gives away, and not a disagreement between commands

reading: They did not, in one place. An object decode counted a payload it could not use against what it delivered, and `verify` never asked: three rounds of the first 60 000 gave a stream that `decode --format damf` exited 7 on, saying that `oadec verify` reports the same faults, and that `verify` called clean. `verify` makes the refusals of the object outputs now, and every other command takes its verdict as before. No stream of the corpus has such a payload, 261 064 payloads in 64 streams, and over 125 streams the binary before and the binary after give the same reports but for the two fields that were added and the same 103 362 691 041 bytes of deliveries. With that put right, 400 000 rounds over 86 streams, two seeds, end without a panic and without a clause broken, and so does every one of the 2 194 352 streams that are one bit away from those 86. What was seen besides is counted and not claimed: what the policy lets one command say and another not, two things `verify` has no rule for, and how much of a changed stream goes through every command once its checksums are put right.
